tn.translation: To simplify reading, we chose to mark only the high tone and the modulated tones (falling and rising). The existence of a downstep (lowered high tone) is signalled by a downward-pointing arrow (↓). ... 4381.dloc: Part I ch. 3 'Stress', §3.1 and §3.1.1 (A) 'Demarcative Stress in Simple Words', p. 43; §1.4 'The Structure of the Syllable', p. 30; §3.2 'Stress Shifting - Definitive Stress', p. 52 and p. 56; secondary-stress restrictions and clitics p. 44; affixes, reduplication, compounds pp. 45-49; fast speech §3.1.2 pp. 49-52; emphatic stress §3.3 pp. 56-58.
4381.heavy: No weight criterion is named; the rule counts vowels: every vowel is a syllable and long vowels/identical-vowel sequences are 'regarded as consisting of two syllables' (p. 30), so a word-final long vowel takes the primary stress on its first mora, the word's penultimate mora (poo [pó:], kulii [kulí:], letioo [lètió:]), which in syllable terms is stress on a final long-vowelled syllable; a non-final long vowel can carry the stress on its second mora (hoosi [hoó·si]). Extensionally heavy = long vowel (CVV); the language has only (C)V syllables (no codas, p. 30), so closed syllables play no role; vowel quality plays no role.
4381.prule: Primary stress falls 'fixedly on the second-to-last vowel' of the phonological word, every vowel counting as one syllable (all (C)VV sequences, including long vowels, are two syllables, p. 30): i.e. a penultimate-mora rule. A word-final long vowel therefore carries the primary stress on its first half, the word's penultimate mora (poo [pó:], kulii [kulí:], letioo [lètió:]; contrast the definite forms with the stress shifted to the last vowel, poó [poó·], p. 52); a non-final long vowel whose second half is the penultimate vowel is stressed on that second half with Tongan-type breaking (hoosi [hoó·si] or [hoó·ʃi]); otherwise stress is on the penultimate syllable (pato [pá·to], fafine [fafí·ne]). In syllable terms: final syllable if it contains a long vowel, else penult. Monosyllabic words and monosyllabic affixes never form phonological words alone but attach to a neighbour, so the deictics ni/na, person determiners ke/ne, articles te/he and monosyllabic suffixes pull the primary stress one vowel rightward (fale [fá·le] but fale ni [falé·-ni]; nofo but nofo-'i [nofó·-ʔi]); bisyllabic affixes, each member of a compound or base-modifier sequence, and Type I reduplicants form their own phonological words with their own stress. Stated for slow (deliberate) speech; in fast speech non-phrase-final primary stresses reduce to secondary (pp. 49-52).
4381.srule: Secondary stress on every other vowel preceding the primary ('as a basic rule, every other preceding vowel': pasikala [pàsikála], siokaalafi, letioo [lètió:]); it never falls on the second vowel of a long vowel or of a rising VV sequence, nor normally on an inserted /i/ in loans, and then skips to the preceding vowel (tooketaa [tò:ketá:], taaupo'ou, Melipoane, tikisinale); monosyllabic prefixes take it only if the stem's first vowel is unstressed (fè-kúmi).

4384.tone: The source treats Nkoroo's word prosody entirely as tone: 'Nkoroo is a two-tone plus downstep language' (p. 449) with a lexical minimal triple HH / H!H / HL. 'Accentual' (pp. 447, 449, 465; handout p. 1 and p. 11) is used in Williamson's (1978) Ijoid sense of a drift toward fixed tonal melodies on morphosyntactic units, and the published version puts "accentual" in scare quotes on p. 449; it is not a stress or pitch-accent-placement claim. The words 'stress' and 'accent placement' occur nowhere in any held Nkoroo file (a full-text search of all five text files: 'accent' only inside 'accentual'). Obikudo 2008 p. 5 independently: 'Like the other Eastern Ijoid lects, Nkoroo operates a register tone system made up of two level tones, a high and a low plus a downstepped high.' Handout p. 1 (verbatim): 'However, the evidence presented here shows that while Nkoroo has moved in the direction of an accentual system, Defaka remains a true tone system, with some structural borrowing from Nkoroo.' and 'Both Defaka and Nkoroo are two-tone plus downstep languages.'

Kashoki & Mann 1978:70-71, a sketch of Zambian Bantu with Nkoya in its Group H, say of Zambian languages generally that syllables are 'more or less evenly stressed', that any penultimate force (e.g. Cewa) may be an effect of penultimate vowel lengthening, that 'stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish words from each other in meaning', and that 'each of their syllables carries tone' with two contrastive tones, high and low. Yukawa's 'no long vowel' remark means the penultimate-lengthening correlate does not obviously apply to Nkoya.

4391.dq: No published description of Nokuku phonology exists, but my own investigation together with the sources listed suggests the following phonemic inventory.
4391.dloc: Clark 2009 p. 25 'Phonemes and spelling'; p. 27 'Changes: Vowels'; p. 16 sec. 2.1.3. Ray 1926 p. 384 sec. I 'Alphabet' §§1-2.
4391.prule: No synchronic word-stress rule is stated for Nokuku in any reachable source. Clark's 'Stressed (penultimate)' / 'Pre-stress (antepenultimate)' label the Proto-North-Central-Vanuatu vowel positions in a diachronic account of vowel changes (PNCV stress reconstructed as penultimate, p. 16); present-day Nokuku has lost post-consonantal final vowels, so the historic penult is word-final in ʔɔm, ɔv, perɔw, vetɔl, pekur, venu, melum and penultimate only in vowel-final forms (kenia, ovua, notuna). Where present-day stress falls is not said.

4392.quote: またトーンの體系は H, L, R1, R2 の四つの對立をもつ特徵がある。R に二種類が認められ、後續語の基調が低く設定されるものと高く設定されるものがある。 [...] まだ資料が少ないためか、他の東シンブー諸方言と比較する際にトーンの規則的な對應がうまく見出せない。今後も調査を續けたい。 (p. 179) — sec. 2.4 (p. 163): シンブー諸語はおそらく全てがトーン言語で、語を領域とするメロディーが辨別的であると考へられる。 [...] 東シンブー諸語のトーンは音韻的には語を領域とする對立するメロディーである。メロディーのパタンは高 (high)、下降 (falling)、上昇 (rising)、低 (low)、落調 (key-lowering trigger) の五種類にまとめることができる。 (pp. 163-164) — fn. 3 (p. 164): ノマネ地區の諸方言やグナアについてはトーン對立の在り方がまだ充分に明らかになつたとは言へない。これら方言にはさらに別のメロディー/タイプをトーン音素として認める必要があるが、本稿では扱はない。

4392.tone: The source (a comparative subgrouping study built on the author's own fieldwork with Kewa-Meba and Megne speakers, acknowledgements p. 182) treats all Simbu languages as tone languages whose contrastive melodies have the word as their domain (p. 163). For the Nomane group it states a four-way contrast H, L, R1, R2, the two rising tones distinguished by the register they impose on the following word (p. 179); fn. 3 (p. 164) says the tone contrasts of the Nomane-area dialects are not yet sufficiently clear and further melodies/types would have to be recognized; regular tone correspondences with the other East Simbu varieties could not yet be found (p. 179); Nomane is excluded from the correspondence table for that reason (p. 165). General East Simbu tendency (p. 165): longer words carry contour melodies, shorter words level melodies. The text contains no occurrence of アクセント, 強勢, ストレス, 'stress' or 'accent' (a full-text search), so no stress or accent statement exists in the source.

4393.dq: The primary passage does not say whether the pitch contrast / accent is word- or phrase-level ('Nonuya appears to have contrastive pitch similar to Ocaina'). The supporting first-hand sources describe lexical, syllable-scoped tone with word minimal pairs: Echeverri & Romero 2016: 148 'El tono tiene alcance silábico y tiene estatus fonológico hasta donde lo hemos podido establecer.'
4393.dloc: §2.3 Prosody, p. 10; cf. §3.1 p. 11 and Conclusions p. 66.
4393.prule: No stress-placement rule is stated. Nonuya is described as having contrastive pitch (rising and falling tones co-occurring with lengthened vowels; per the supporting sources also distinct level tones on geminate or glottal-separated vowels) and is tentatively typologized as a pitch-accent language.
4393.quote: While Murui and Mɨka have fixed stress position (word-initial) (Wojtylak 2021a–b), Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode appear to have meaningful contrasts between words according to tonal contours ... Nonuya appears to have contrastive pitch similar to Ocaina (Orjuela Salinas 2010). Ascending and descending tones regularly tend to co-occur with lengthened vowels. Hyman (2016: 236) places “Huitoto” (Murui-Muina) within “other tonal systems” with a question mark. Wetzels and Meira (2010: 345–346), based on Aschmann’s (1993) data, tentatively hypothesize that Ocaina is a “non-stress [i.e., pitch] accent language”…
4393.loc: §2.3 Prosody, p. 10; cf. §3.1 p. 11 and Conclusions p. 66.
4393.idn: Nonuya (nonu1241), one of the three extant Witotoan languages ('Murui-Muina... (nucl1659), Ocaina (Okaina, ocai1244), and Nonuya (nonu1241)', §1.1 p. 1); no dialect named. Data: a documentation corpus of 8,689 entries recorded from four speakers 1973-2007 (Mamerto Ríos, Humberto Ayarce, Rafael Grande, Margarita Kapojó), §1.1 p. 4; location: 'The few Nonuya speakers reside in a community in the Caquetá River in Colombia', §1.2 p. 5.
4393.tone: Chapter §2.3 (p. 10): 'Nonuya appears to have contrastive pitch similar to Ocaina (Orjuela Salinas 2010). Ascending and descending tones regularly tend to co-occur with lengthened vowels.'... 'we suggest that Ocaina, Nonuya, and the Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode dialects of Murui-Muina may be typologized as pitch-accent languages'; Conclusions p. 66: 'In relation to prosody, Ocaina, Nonuya, and of the Mɨnɨka and Nɨpode dialects of Murui-Muina appear to have pitch-accent systems.' §3.1 p. 11 lists 'accent (Murui-Muina, Ocaina, Nonuya)' among morphemes realized as suprasegmentals. Wojtylak 2016 handout p. 7: 'Nonuya has two tonal distinctions (similar to Ocaina, but distinct from Witoto)' and 'Complex rules of stress assignment (there are no unified stress patterns across Witotoan languages)' - no placement given. Romero Cruz 2015a: 74: 'Landaburu y Echeverri (ms. s f.) así como Orjuela (2010) afirman que el nononotá es una lengua tonal.' Echeverri & Romero 2016: 147-148: rising/falling tones with vowel lengthening, distinct level tones on geminate or glottal-separated vowels, 'El tono tiene alcance silábico y tiene estatus fonológico'; implosives /ɓ ɗ/ 'se realizan como [b] y [d] en sílabas no acentuadas' (a stressed/unstressed distinction is assumed but never located). No source gives a stress-placement rule; the only fixed-stress statement in §2.3 (word-initial) is for Murui and Mɨka, not Nonuya.

4394.prule: No positional rule is stated. Stress /´/ is listed as a phoneme in the inventory (p. 86). Primary-stress position is reported only as attested pattern frequencies taken from Amoss 1961:15: ŚS̀ most common, ŚS less common, S...Ś possible, S̀Ś occurs, Ś₁Ś₂ when S₂ is a stressed suffix (double primary stress allowed); monosyllables regularly carry primary stress in isolation. Primary stress = raised relative pitch plus about 1/2 mora of added length (one mora at slow tempo); lack of stress dulls vowel quality.
4394.srule: Secondary stress [ˋ] (raised pitch without added length) is rare, optional and non-phonemic at word level: where it occurs in citation forms it is 'analyzable as optionally present or absent (for example in the environments _SŚ and ŚS(S)_)'; Galloway (with L. Thompson and B. Efrat) did not find Amoss's ŚS̀, ŚS̀S̀ or S̀Ś patterns; 'at word level [ˋ] is predictable and non-phonemic'. At sentence level [ˋ] is more frequent but is an allophone of /´/ on monosyllables adjacent to stressed words.
